title: Glacial Collapse Floods Kill Over 390 on Nepal-Tibet Border as Iran War Hits Six Months With No Off-Ramp
subhead: A Himalayan glacier collapse unleashed catastrophic floods that killed more than 390 people and left over 1,400 missing across the Nepal-China border, while the US-Iran war reached its six-month mark with diplomacy intensifying but no end in sight.

sections.heading: Himalayan Glacier Collapse Kills Over 390, Leaves 1,400 Missing
sections.body:
Catastrophic flash floods triggered by a glacial collapse swept through communities along the Nepal-China border on Wednesday, killing more than 390 people and leaving over 1,400 missing, according to police and rescue officials cited by the Associated Press. The US Geological Survey said the flooding was triggered by a glacial collapse, and scientists' preliminary investigations point to rapidly melting Himalayan ice as the cause, the BBC reports. CCTV footage showed a wall of water and mud several stories high sweeping through Gyirong Port near the border.

The disaster has an unusually international dimension: people from more than 30 countries are among the missing, AP reports, and South Korea has dispatched a rapid response team to Nepal as its citizens remain unaccounted for. Rescuers on both sides of the border are searching for survivors while bracing for the possibility of a second flood, with the BBC reporting that fears of another surge have put rescue teams on edge.
sections.whyItMatters: The disaster underscores the accelerating risk of Himalayan glacial collapse as a regional security and humanitarian threat, striking a border zone where China and Nepal must coordinate a cross-border response at a moment of heightened great-power tension.

sections.heading: Iran War Reaches Six Months With No Off-Ramp as Mediators Converge on Tehran
sections.body:
The US-Iran war reached its six-month mark on Friday with no end in sight, despite President Donald Trump's initial forecast that it would last four to five weeks, according to an AP review. A June memorandum of understanding that briefly paused hostilities has expired, and White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said Thursday that 'no negotiations are happening right now.' The Strait of Hormuz, through which more than one-fifth of global oil and gas supplies once passed, has been largely closed since early March, with traffic down roughly 95 percent, Al Jazeera reports.

Yet a flurry of high-level visits to Tehran suggests a renewed push for talks. Qatar's Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani is in Tehran on Thursday to discuss de-escalation and reviving failed negotiations, Al Jazeera reports, following visits by Pakistan's army chief Asim Munir and Oman's Foreign Minister Badr Albusaidi. Iran and Oman have agreed on a temporary shipping route through the strait, and Qatar has stressed the need for the waterway to return to its pre-February 28 status. Washington, meanwhile, has pivoted from strikes to economic pressure, threatening to sanction countries that refuse to break trade ties with Iran, AP reports.
sections.whyItMatters: Six months in, the war has outlasted every official forecast, and the combination of a closed Hormuz, depleted US munitions and a new mediation push makes the coming weeks pivotal for whether the conflict de-escalates or hardens into a longer economic siege.

sections.heading: US Patriot Missile Stocks in Europe 'Beyond Critical' After Iran War Drawdown
sections.body:
The US military is experiencing a 'beyond critical' shortage of advanced missile interceptors in Europe, largely driven by the war with Iran, a US defense official in Europe and a NATO official told the Associated Press. The most concerning shortfall involves Patriot interceptors, which can shoot down Russia's high-speed ballistic missiles. US missile stocks in Europe have been moved to the Middle East, where US and Gulf allies have fired significant numbers of interceptors to thwart Iranian drones and missiles.

The officials warned that in the event of a Russian ballistic missile assault on a NATO target, the alliance could be forced 'to take punch after punch in the mouth,' in the words of the US defense official, and would have 'very limited' capability to defend against even a single ballistic missile strike. Though a Russian attack on NATO is not imminently expected, the shortfall exposes a vulnerability in European air defense at a moment when the CIA director's secret trip to Moscow has opened a new channel between Washington and the Kremlin, the BBC notes.
sections.whyItMatters: The Iran war has quietly hollowed out NATO's missile defense in Europe, creating a strategic vulnerability that Moscow could exploit and that will take years of production to repair.

sections.heading: Chad Accuses Sudan of Cross-Border Air Strike Killing 12, Widening the Sahel War
sections.body:
Chad has accused Sudan's army of launching an air strike on a fuel market near their shared border that killed at least 12 people and wounded seven, Al Jazeera reports, citing a Chadian security source who said the strike targeted a site where the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) refuel. The US embassy in Khartoum backed Chad's account, condemning the Sudanese army for the strikes on Thursday. Sudan's Foreign Ministry said it was surprised by the allegations and insisted its forces respect the sovereignty of its neighbours.

The incident follows a Chadian claim last week that Sudan struck a military convoy more than 100km inside its territory in the eastern Ennedi region. Chad has raised its alert level to its highest point and deployed about 100 armoured vehicles and signal-jamming trucks near the border, a local source told Reuters. The strike comes against the backdrop of a Sudanese civil war between the army and the RSF that has lasted over three years and displaced millions, and which the UN warns threatens an entire generation.
sections.whyItMatters: The Sudan war is spilling across borders into Chad, threatening to draw a second state into a regional conflict that already destabilises the Sahel and the Red Sea approaches, and complicating Washington's push for an arms embargo on Khartoum.

sections.heading: Gaza Ceasefire at Risk of Collapse, Board of Peace Envoy Warns
sections.body:
A senior official on President Trump's Board of Peace has warned that a collapse of last October's Gaza ceasefire would be 'a point of no return' for the region, the BBC reports. Nickolay Mladenov, the Board's high representative for Gaza, told the UN Security Council that Israel's continuing air strikes and Hamas's incomplete disarmament both threaten the process. Israel has rejected the 15-point roadmap for Hamas's disarmament announced by the Board last month, insisting the group must fully disarm before any troop withdrawal, while Hamas has agreed to give up weapons in exchange for a phased Israeli pullout.

At least 1,303 Palestinians, including 300 children, have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza since the ceasefire began, according to the Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures the UN considers reliable. Mladenov said the process had not stalled and that committees had been established to settle remaining questions, but warned that 'every use of force that does not answer an immediate threat' costs the process something hard to buy back. His account differs from that of Trump envoy Jared Kushner, who said after meeting Israel's prime minister that withdrawal would be discussed only once demilitarisation was 'done.'
sections.whyItMatters: The ceasefire that ended the Gaza war is fraying over the sequencing of disarmament and withdrawal, and a collapse would reignite a conflict that has already killed more than 1,300 people since the truce began.

sections.heading: Trump Renames Lake Ontario 'Lake America' as US-Canada Trade War Deepens
sections.body:
President Donald Trump signed an executive order Thursday renaming Lake Ontario 'Lake America' for the US geographic naming service, the Associated Press reports, in a symbolic escalation of his trade war with Canada. The order comes after trade talks between the US and Canada collapsed late last week, the BBC notes. The renaming follows a series of escalating measures in the bilateral dispute, which has already seen Trump impose steep tariffs on Canadian goods and threats over energy exports.

The move is largely symbolic — the lake is shared with Canada, which will not recognise the new name — but it signals the administration's willingness to escalate a dispute with its largest trading partner and closest ally. Canada has responded to earlier US tariffs with its own measures, and the collapse of talks has left the two economies in a state of heightened uncertainty over trade, energy and border issues.
sections.whyItMatters: A dispute with Washington's closest ally and largest trading partner has moved from tariffs to symbolic territorial gestures, underscoring how far the US-Canada relationship has deteriorated and the economic risk that carries for both sides.

bottomLine: Today's dominant story is humanitarian: a Himalayan glacial collapse killed more than 390 people and left over 1,400 missing across the Nepal-China border, with citizens of more than 30 countries unaccounted for. Strategically, the US-Iran war passed its six-month mark with no off-ramp, even as Qatari, Omani and Pakistani mediators converged on Tehran and Washington's economic squeeze on Iran tightened — while the war's cost became visible in a 'beyond critical' Patriot missile shortage in Europe. The Sudan war is spilling into Chad, the Gaza ceasefire is fraying over disarmament sequencing, and the US-Canada trade war has escalated into symbolic territory. The common thread is a world in which multiple crises are compounding: a closed Hormuz, depleted Western munitions, and a cascade of regional conflicts that no single off-ramp yet resolves.
